results.summary: Tech-lead review found one zero-tolerance prohibited-pattern violation and three maintainability/consistency risks. API layering is broadly sound, but the Optional.get usage must be removed before this passes the agent’s prohibited-pattern checklist.

findings.title: Optional.get() remains in production authentication filter
findings.description: The bearer-token filter validates that the Optional is non-empty, but then calls Optional.get() twice. The tech-lead prohibited-pattern checklist flags Optional.get() calls as zero-tolerance because later refactors can easily separate the check from the access and turn this into a NoSuchElementException in the auth path.
findings.evidence: Optional<AdminUserDto> user is checked at lines 56-61, then dereferenced with user.get() at lines 64 and 66.
findings.suggestedFix: Assign the value once with an explicit safe extraction after validation, for example: AdminUserDto adminUser = user.orElseThrow(); then use adminUser and adminUser.role(), or restructure validateToken(token).map(...).orElseGet(...) without get().

findings.title: Zero-hit demand rules are duplicated across domain, entity, and native SQL
findings.description: Priority thresholds and opportunity-loss calculation are encoded in multiple places: the domain decider, the entity invariant helper, and the PostgreSQL upsert CASE/expression. The behavior is currently aligned, but a threshold or rounding change can drift between PostgreSQL and JPA fallback paths.
findings.evidence: Native SQL calculates loss and priority at lines 50-56; ZeroHitPriorityDecider repeats thresholds at src/main/java/com/skishop/domain/ZeroHitPriorityDecider.java:20 and :23; ZeroHitSearch repeats them at src/main/java/com/skishop/entity/ZeroHitSearch.java:167-175.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the Java priority rule a single source, such as Priority.fromHitCount(int), and ensure both entity and service use it. If the native SQL upsert remains for concurrency, add a focused contract test that proves SQL and Java policy stay aligned for boundary hit counts and rounding.

findings.title: Repository adapter is packaged under service layer
findings.description: ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway is a data-access adapter: it is annotated @Repository, uses NamedParameterJdbcTemplate and DataSource, and queries ZeroHitSearchRepository. Keeping it under com.skishop.service blurs the service/repository boundary defined by the Java AGENTS instructions and backend design layering.
findings.evidence: package com.skishop.service at line 1; @Repository at line 20; JDBC/DataSource dependencies at lines 59-61.
findings.suggestedFix: Move this class to com.skishop.repository or an infrastructure.persistence package, then inject it into ZeroHitRecordingService as a persistence gateway. Keep application orchestration in service and SQL/JDBC concerns in the persistence layer.

findings.title: Coverage target is reported but not enforced by Maven
findings.description: The AGENTS quality bar targets at least 80% line and branch coverage. pom.xml configures JaCoCo report generation only, so mvn verify can pass even if future changes drop coverage below the OSS bar.
findings.evidence: jacoco-maven-plugin has prepare-agent and report executions, but no check execution or LINE/BRANCH minimum limits.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a jacoco:check execution in verify with LINE and BRANCH COVEREDRATIO minimums of 0.80, or document why the project intentionally keeps coverage as report-only.

escalations.description: Decide whether the PostgreSQL-native upsert should remain despite duplicated business rules. It provides concurrency value, but the project needs an explicit policy for keeping SQL and Java demand calculations aligned.

designDeviations.description: A data-access class annotated @Repository is located in the service package, weakening the Controller -> Service -> Repository layer separation.

findings.title: Repository infrastructure is implemented inside the service package
findings.description: `ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway` is declared in `com.skishop.service` but is annotated with `@Repository`, owns native SQL/JDBC access, injects `DataSource`, and calls `ZeroHitSearchRepository`. findings.evidence: Line 1 declares `package com.skishop.service;`; line 15 imports `org.springframework.stereotype.Repository`; line 20 annotates the class with `@Repository`.
findings.suggestedFix: Move this class to `com.skishop.repository` or a clearly named infrastructure package. If the service needs an abstraction, define a service-facing gateway interface and keep the JDBC implementation outside `service/`.

findings.title: Required package layout is not implemented for model and DTO subpackages
findings.description: The architecture checklist expects JPA entities under `model/` and DTOs split into `dto/request/` and `dto/response/`. The implementation uses `entity/` for JPA entities and a flat `dto/` package for request and response records.
findings.evidence: `Product.java` declares `package com.skishop.entity;` and is annotated with `@Entity`; request/response DTOs such as `AiConsultRequest` and `AiConsultResponse` declare `package com.skishop.dto;`.

findings.title: Response DTO is coupled to an entity-package enum
findings.description: `ZeroHitItemDto` imports `com.skishop.entity.Priority` and exposes it as an API response field. Even though `Priority` is not itself a JPA entity, this couples the frontend API contract to the persistence/model package and allows model changes to leak past the service boundary.
findings.evidence: Line 3 imports `com.skishop.entity.Priority`; line 17 exposes `Priority priority` in the DTO record.
findings.suggestedFix: Expose an API-owned enum/string in the DTO package, or move `Priority` into a domain/API-neutral package if it is intended to be shared outside persistence.

findings.title: Environment profile separation is incomplete
findings.description: Configuration is split into `application.yml`, `application-docker.yml`, and test resources, but the expected dev/prod profile separation is absent. Common config also contains datasource and JPA settings directly, making production-vs-development behavior less explicit.
findings.evidence: `application.yml` defines datasource and `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: validate`; no `application-dev.yml` or `application-prod.yml` is present in the reviewed target files.
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce explicit `application-dev.yml` and `application-prod.yml` profiles, keep shared defaults in `application.yml`, and document profile selection. Configure JPA logging/dialect behavior intentionally per profile where needed.

findings.title: Auth request metadata parsing is embedded in the controller
findings.description: `AuthController` extracts source IP from proxy headers with conditional logic and passes it into the authentication use case. This is HTTP/auth cross-cutting concern logic inside a controller rather than a centralized filter, resolver, or request-context component.
findings.evidence: `sourceIp(HttpServletRequest request)` checks `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP`, and `getRemoteAddr()` directly in the controller.
findings.suggestedFix: Move source-IP resolution to a dedicated component, filter, or argument resolver and inject/use that from the controller or authentication service.

escalations.description: Decide whether the canonical package convention is the agent-defined `model/` + `dto/request|response/` structure or the current `entity/` + flat `dto/` structure. If the current structure is intentional, update the architecture standard to prevent false-positive reviews.

results.summary: DDD domain review failed due to high-severity domain modeling issues: inter-aggregate coordination is implemented as direct service calls instead of domain events, PostgreSQL upsert bypasses the ZeroHitSearch aggregate and duplicates business rules in SQL, monetary concepts are primitive BigDecimal fields rather than value objects, and Product invariants are not enforced in the entity constructor.

findings.title: Product search coordinates ZeroHitSearch directly instead of publishing a domain event
findings.description: ProductSearchService queries Product and, when totalCount is zero, directly calls ZeroHitRecordingService.record(...) inside the same application service. No ApplicationEventPublisher or event listener exists in src/main/java. Under the agent checklist, inter-aggregate coordination should be event-driven, e.g. ProductSearchReturnedZeroResultsEvent handled by a Zero Hit listener, so the Product search use case does not directly invoke the ZeroHitSearch aggregate workflow.
findings.evidence: Line 24 injects ZeroHitRecordingService; lines 63-64 call zeroHitRecordingService.record(trimmedKeyword). Repository-wide search found no ApplicationEventPublisher, @EventListener, or @TransactionalEventListener usage.
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce an immutable past-tense event such as ProductSearchReturnedZeroResultsEvent(String keyword, Instant searchedAt). ProductSearchService should publish it via ApplicationEventPublisher after determining zero results; a ZeroHit event handler should call ZeroHitRecordingService, using @TransactionalEventListener where post-commit behavior is required.

findings.title: PostgreSQL atomic upsert bypasses aggregate methods and duplicates domain rules in SQL
findings.description: ZeroHitAtomicUpsertGateway mutates zero_hit_searches directly with JDBC and calculates hit_count, priority, and estimated_opportunity_loss in SQL. This bypasses ZeroHitSearch.firstHit/recordRepeat and duplicates ZeroHitPriorityDecider/OpportunityLossCalculator logic, so future threshold or loss formula changes can silently diverge between Java domain behavior and the PostgreSQL path.
findings.evidence: UPSERT_SQL inserts LOW priority, increments hit_count, recalculates estimated_opportunity_loss from avg(price), and hard-codes HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW thresholds in CASE expressions.
findings.suggestedFix: Keep concurrency handling in persistence infrastructure but route business state transitions through the aggregate. Prefer a custom repository using row-level/advisory locking or unique-constraint retry that loads/creates ZeroHitSearch and calls firstHit/recordRepeat. If native SQL remains, centralize and test the invariant mapping explicitly against the domain policy for every threshold.

findings.title: Money-like concepts are persisted as raw BigDecimal instead of immutable value objects
findings.description: Product.price and ZeroHitSearch.estimatedOpportunityLoss are core monetary domain concepts, but they are modeled directly as BigDecimal fields. The DDD checklist expects value objects such as Money to be immutable records with self-validation and embedded persistence mapping. Current validation is split across entity constructors, SQL constraints, and calculators, with no currency/scale invariant in a single value type.
findings.evidence: Product.price is BigDecimal at lines 40-41; ZeroHitSearch.estimatedOpportunityLoss is BigDecimal at src/main/java/com/skishop/entity/ZeroHitSearch.java:40-41; ZeroHitDemandSignals exposes BigDecimal at src/main/java/com/skishop/domain/ZeroHitDemandSignals.java:10.
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce a Money value object, for example an @Embeddable record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) with non-negative, scale, and currency validation. Embed it in Product and ZeroHitSearch with AttributeOverrides and have OpportunityLossCalculator return Money rather than BigDecimal.

findings.title: Product aggregate constructor does not enforce product invariants
findings.description: Product is documented as read-only seed data, but its public constructor is also documented for tests and future admin tooling. It only uses Objects.requireNonNull for manufacturer, name, category, description, price, and stockStatus, so blank text and negative prices can enter the domain object until database constraints reject them. Domain invariants should be enforced when the aggregate is created, not delegated to persistence.
findings.evidence: Lines 73-79 assign required fields with Objects.requireNonNull only. The database separately enforces price >= 0 in src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_products_and_zero_hit_searches.sql:13.
findings.suggestedFix: Add Product factory/constructor validation for non-blank manufacturer/name/category/description, non-negative price or Money, valid stockStatus, and timestamp ordering. Keep database constraints as a backstop, not the first line of domain protection.

escalations.description: The backend sandbox only exposed backend/AGENTS.md; referenced parent design docs and Java AGENTS instructions were outside the readable workspace. This review therefore relies on the supplied instructions and source evidence only.

results.summary: API endpoint review found no legacy .do mappings and the implemented /api endpoints mostly match the REST design, but there are high-impact issues around GET side effects, trusted forwarded IP handling on login, and non-RFC9457 error payloads.

findings.title: GET /api/products/search records zero-hit data as a side effect
findings.description: The public search endpoint is implemented as GET, but the service records zero-result searches when no products match. GET requests must be safe; browser prefetching, crawlers, caches, retries, or shared links can inflate zero-hit demand metrics without a deliberate user action.
findings.evidence: @GetMapping("/search") delegates to productSearchUseCase.search(...). ProductSearchService then calls zeroHitRecordingService.record(trimmedKeyword) when totalCount == 0 at src/main/java/com/skishop/service/ProductSearchService.java:63-64.
findings.suggestedFix: Split read and write behavior: keep GET /api/products/search read-only, and record search events through a POST endpoint such as /api/search-events or /api/zero-hit-searches after an explicit frontend search. If the design intentionally keeps analytics recording on GET, add a documented exception and cache-control protections, but the REST risk remains.

findings.title: Login rate limiting trusts spoofable X-Forwarded-For and X-Real-IP headers
findings.description: AuthController accepts client-supplied forwarding headers without validating that the request came through a trusted proxy. Because the login limiter keys attempts by username and sourceIp, an attacker can rotate X-Forwarded-For values and avoid per-source lockout for the same username.
findings.evidence: sourceIp() returns X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP directly. AdminAuthService.login passes sourceIp to loginAttemptLimiter.isAllowed(...) at line 64, and InMemoryLoginAttemptLimiter builds the key from username + sourceIp at src/main/java/com/skishop/service/InMemoryLoginAttemptLimiter.java:54-59.
findings.suggestedFix: Use request.getRemoteAddr() by default. Only honor forwarded headers when Spring is configured for trusted proxies, validate the extracted address as a single IP, cap its length, and ignore arbitrary client-supplied chains.

findings.title: LoginRequest lacks length constraints for externally supplied credentials
findings.description: The login body is annotated with @NotBlank but has no @Size constraints. Very large username or password values still pass Bean Validation and reach the auth service, password encoder, and rate-limiter key path. The server request-size limit reduces blast radius but does not replace field-level API validation.
findings.evidence: public record LoginRequest(@NotBlank String username, @NotBlank String password)
findings.suggestedFix: Add bounded constraints, for example @NotBlank @Size(max = 255) for username and @NotBlank @Size(max = 128) or an agreed maximum for password. If username is always an email, add @Email as well.

findings.title: Global API errors do not use Spring Boot 3.2 ProblemDetail / RFC 9457 format
findings.description: The global handler returns a custom ApiErrorResponse record through ResponseEntity instead of Spring's ProblemDetail or ResponseEntityExceptionHandler flow. This misses the RFC 9457 shape expected by the review standard and makes interoperability with standard problem clients harder.
findings.evidence: Handlers return ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse>; ApiErrorResponse is a custom record at src/main/java/com/skishop/exception/ApiErrorResponse.java:16-23. No ProblemDetail or ResponseEntityExceptionHandler usage was found.
findings.suggestedFix: Migrate the advice to return ProblemDetail, setting type/title/status/detail/instance and adding extension properties such as code and errors. If the frontend contract must retain the current payload, document that as a deliberate deviation from RFC 9457.

findings.title: Admin controllers lack class-level base @RequestMapping
findings.description: AdminZeroHitController and AiConsultController put the full /api/admin/... path on each method and do not define a controller-level @RequestMapping base path. The endpoint behavior is currently correct, but it violates the controller base-path convention and makes future admin route additions easier to drift.
findings.evidence: AdminZeroHitController has @RestController and @GetMapping("/api/admin/zero-hits") without @RequestMapping("/api/admin"). AiConsultController similarly uses @PostMapping("/api/admin/ai-consult") at src/main/java/com/skishop/controller/AiConsultController.java:16-31.
findings.suggestedFix: Add @RequestMapping("/api/admin") to both admin controllers, then change method mappings to /zero-hits and /ai-consult. This keeps mappings identical while enforcing a consistent admin namespace.

escalations.description: The backend design explicitly says GET /api/products/search records zero-hit searches, but REST endpoint review treats GET side effects as a high-risk convention violation. A product/API owner should decide whether to revise the API contract or document this as an intentional analytics exception.
Decide whether the frontend contract should keep the custom ApiErrorResponse shape or migrate to RFC 9457 ProblemDetail with extension fields.

results.summary: Async/concurrency review found blocking and shared-state risks: synchronized database I/O, missing Java 21 virtual-thread enablement, transaction scope held across external AI I/O, and non-atomic in-memory auth invariants.

findings.title: JPA database I/O is executed inside a synchronized block
findings.description: The H2/non-PostgreSQL fallback path enters a JVM monitor and then performs repository read/update/insert operations. Under Java 21 virtual threads this can pin carrier threads while JDBC blocks, and even on platform threads it serializes all zero-hit writes through one singleton lock. This is especially risky because the fallback method runs inside a TransactionTemplate started before the monitor is acquired.
findings.evidence: synchronized (fallbackUpsertLock) wraps zeroHitSearchRepository.findByNormalizedKeyword(...), updateExisting(...), insertFirst(...), and those paths call zeroHitSearchRepository.save(...).
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the monitor-based read-modify-write fallback. Prefer an atomic database operation per supported database, or handle the unique constraint with a retry in a fresh transaction. If a local lock remains unavoidable, use ReentrantLock and keep DB I/O outside the locked section as much as possible.

findings.title: Database metadata I/O is performed while holding a synchronized monitor
findings.description: supportsAtomicUpsert() performs DataSource connection acquisition and database metadata lookup inside synchronized (this). With virtual threads enabled, blocking JDBC work inside a synchronized section can pin a carrier thread. The first request hitting this path can also serialize concurrent zero-hit recording requests behind metadata I/O.
findings.evidence: Line 83 calls databaseProductName() while inside synchronized; databaseProductName() opens a JDBC connection and reads DatabaseMetaData at lines 105-107.
findings.suggestedFix: Initialize database support eagerly at startup, or use a ReentrantLock/future-style initializer that does not hold a JVM monitor across JDBC I/O. Keep connection acquisition outside synchronized blocks.

findings.title: Java 21 virtual threads are not enabled in runtime configuration
findings.description: The project targets Java 21 and uses Spring Boot 3.2.x, but no application profile sets spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. Synchronous controller paths currently perform JPA and Spring AI calls on servlet platform threads, increasing risk of Tomcat worker exhaustion under slow DB or AI calls.
findings.evidence: Search for spring.threads/virtual returned no matches in src/main/resources, src/test/resources, pom.xml, or Dockerfile. application.yml defines spring.datasource, jpa, flyway, ai, but no spring.threads.virtual.enabled.
findings.suggestedFix: After removing synchronized-over-I/O pinning hazards, add `spring.threads.virtual.enabled: true` to the default and Docker runtime configuration. Validate request concurrency with the zero-hit and AI endpoints.

findings.title: External AI provider call runs inside a read-only transaction
findings.description: AiConsultationService opens a read-only transaction, loads prompt context from the database, and then calls the AI provider before the transactional method returns. That can keep transaction/EntityManager resources bound while a slow external HTTP call blocks the request thread. With virtual threads disabled this also consumes a Tomcat platform thread for the full provider latency.
findings.evidence: @Transactional(readOnly = true) is applied to consult(); after repository reads at lines 45-47, line 51 calls aiProviderClient.generate(prompt). SpringAiProviderClient.generate() performs blocking chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content() at line 35.
findings.suggestedFix: Limit the transaction to the DB context lookup only, then perform the AI call outside any transaction. For example, move category/manufacturer lookup into a small read-only method and return detached immutable context before invoking aiProviderClient.generate(...).

findings.title: Active admin token limit is not enforced atomically under concurrent logins
findings.description: The in-memory session map is a ConcurrentHashMap, but the max-token invariant is implemented as separate count/remove and put operations. Concurrent successful login requests can all observe fewer than three active tokens and then each insert a new token, exceeding MAX_ACTIVE_TOKENS_PER_ADMIN.
findings.evidence: issueToken() calls enforceActiveTokenLimit(user) at line 126 and only later sessions.put(...) at line 132. enforceActiveTokenLimit() counts sessions at lines 136-139 and removes one at lines 143-146 without a shared atomic boundary around the subsequent put.
findings.suggestedFix: Guard the whole enforce-and-put sequence with a ReentrantLock, or store sessions per admin and update the per-admin token set via a single compute/lock-protected operation. Add a concurrent login test that asserts the cap never exceeds 3.

findings.title: Login attempt rate-limit check and failure recording are split across non-atomic operations
findings.description: Concurrent failed login requests can all pass isAllowed() before any request records its failure. The map update in recordFailure() is atomic by itself, but the overall allow/check/fail sequence is not, so a burst can exceed the intended threshold before the lock takes effect.
findings.evidence: isAllowed() reads attempts.get(...) at lines 31-33. AdminAuthService.login() calls isAllowed() first and only calls recordFailure() later on failed credentials. recordFailure() uses attempts.compute(...) at lines 39-46, but it is not combined with the allow decision.
findings.suggestedFix: Expose a single atomic operation such as `recordFailureIfAllowed(username, sourceIp)` implemented with ConcurrentHashMap.compute(), returning whether the attempt should proceed or be rate-limited. Alternatively serialize per-key limiter updates with a keyed lock.

escalations.description: Decide whether the non-PostgreSQL zero-hit fallback is production-supported. If it is only for tests, remove it from runtime code or isolate it behind test configuration to eliminate monitor-based database I/O.
Confirm the release posture for Java 21 virtual threads. Enabling them is recommended, but should be sequenced after removing synchronized-over-I/O pinning hazards.

results.summary: Exception handling avoids empty catches and client stack-trace disclosure, and log statements generally use SLF4J placeholders without obvious PII. findings.title: No correlation ID filter or MDC propagation is implemented
findings.description: Requests are logged, but the filter does not read or generate X-Correlation-Id, does not put a correlationId into MDC, does not return the ID in the response header, and has no MDC cleanup. Repository-wide search found no MDC, X-Correlation-Id, correlationId, traceId, or spanId usage, so production incidents cannot reliably join logs across a request.
findings.evidence: RequestLoggingFilter only records start time and logs method/path/status/duration in finally. No MDC.put, response.setHeader("X-Correlation-Id", ...), or MDC.clear() appears anywhere in src/main/java or src/main/resources.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a OncePerRequestFilter that reads X-Correlation-Id, generates a UUID when missing, validates/bounds the value, puts it in MDC under correlationId, sets the response header, and clears MDC in finally. Include correlationId in the Logback pattern or JSON fields.

findings.title: Global exception responses do not use ProblemDetail/RFC7807
findings.description: The global handler returns a custom ApiErrorResponse record rather than Spring Boot 3 ProblemDetail. This deviates from the review standard requiring RFC7807/RFC9457 style responses for error payloads.
findings.evidence: Handler methods return ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse>, and build() constructs new ApiErrorResponse(timestamp, status, message, code, path, errors) at lines 125-132. ApiErrorWriter also emits ApiErrorResponse for Spring Security errors.
findings.suggestedFix: Return ProblemDetail from @ExceptionHandler methods, set title/detail/status and stable properties such as code, path, and errors via pd.setProperty(...). Align ApiErrorWriter/security responses with the same ProblemDetail shape.

findings.title: Unexpected exception handler drops the stack trace
findings.description: The catch-all exception handler logs only the request URI and exception class name. Because the Throwable is not passed as the final SLF4J argument, the stack trace and causal chain are lost from server logs exactly when they are most needed.
findings.evidence: LOGGER.error("Unexpected API error at {} with type {}", request.getRequestURI(), exception.getClass().getName());
findings.suggestedFix: Use placeholder logging with the Throwable as the last argument, for example: LOGGER.error("Unexpected API error path={} type={}", request.getRequestURI(), exception.getClass().getName(), exception);

findings.title: Handled AI provider failures are converted to responses without logging the exception
findings.description: AiProviderException is caught and converted to ProviderStatus.ERROR, but the log line records only the status. The original provider failure and stack trace are neither propagated nor logged, making provider outages hard to diagnose.

results.summary: Data access review found several policy violations in entity mapping and persistence configuration. findings.title: java.sql.Timestamp is used in the PostgreSQL upsert gateway

findings.title: Datasource URLs and docker credentials have hardcoded defaults

results.summary: Security review found 2 Critical, 3 High, and 1 Medium findings. The highest-risk issues are a hardcoded Docker-profile database password default and a spoofable login rate-limit key based on untrusted forwarding headers.

findings.title: Docker profile contains a hardcoded default database password
findings.description: The Docker profile uses `${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD:skishop}`, so deployments that omit the environment variable silently run with the public password `skishop`. This violates the repository secret-management rule and makes accidental insecure deployments likely.
findings.evidence: password: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD:skishop}
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the default secret and require `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` to be set, e.g. `password: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD}`. Provide only non-secret placeholders in `.env.example` and fail startup when the value is absent.

findings.category: A01: Broken Access Control / Rate Limiting / Spoofing
findings.title: Login rate limiting can be bypassed by spoofing X-Forwarded-For
findings.description: `AuthController` trusts `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Real-IP` directly, and `InMemoryLoginAttemptLimiter` keys attempts by username plus that source IP. An attacker can rotate these headers on `/api/auth/login` to avoid the 5-failure lockout and continue credential-stuffing attempts.
findings.evidence: sourceIp() returns the first `X-Forwarded-For` value before `request.getRemoteAddr()`. The limiter key is `username + "|" + sourceIp` in `InMemoryLoginAttemptLimiter`.
findings.suggestedFix: Centralize client IP resolution and only honor forwarding headers when `request.getRemoteAddr()` is a trusted reverse proxy. Add a username-only or global throttle in addition to IP-based throttling, and add tests proving spoofed XFF values do not bypass lockout.

findings.category: A09: Security Logging and Monitoring / DoS
findings.title: Login limiter stores unbounded attacker-controlled keys
findings.description: Failed login state is held in a `ConcurrentHashMap` keyed by user-controlled username and source IP. Entries are not evicted after the window expires unless the same key is revisited, so a flood of unique usernames or spoofed IPs can grow memory indefinitely.
findings.evidence: `private final Map<String, AttemptState> attempts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();` with keys derived from nullable username/sourceIp and no max size or scheduled cleanup.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a bounded cache with TTL and maximum size, or periodically purge expired entries. Prefer a distributed/bounded rate limiter for production and avoid unlimited per-identity map growth.

findings.title: Public zero-hit search writes are not rate-limited
findings.description: `GET /api/products/search` is public and records a new zero-hit aggregate whenever a nonblank search has no results. A bot can submit many unique 100-character queries to create unbounded database rows and inflate radar metrics.
findings.evidence: SecurityConfig permits `GET /api/products/search`, and `ProductSearchService` calls `zeroHitRecordingService.record(trimmedKeyword)` for every zero-result keyword without a request/user/IP write limit.
findings.suggestedFix: Add public search rate limiting and a distinct zero-hit write quota per source/window. Consider suppressing low-quality/random keywords and monitoring abnormal distinct-keyword volume.

findings.category: Security Headers / A07: XSS Defense in Depth
findings.title: Expected browser hardening headers are not explicitly configured
findings.description: The security chain does not configure the required CSP, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, or explicit server header suppression. Spring Security defaults cover some headers, but the project standard expects explicit defense-in-depth headers such as `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'`.
findings.evidence: The filter chain configures CSRF/CORS/session/auth handlers but no `.headers(...)`; `application.yml` has server error limits but no `server.server-header=` setting.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `.headers(headers -> headers.contentSecurityPolicy(...).referrerPolicy(...).permissionsPolicy(...))` and explicitly blank/suppress server-identifying headers in configuration. Keep default nosniff/frame/HSTS behavior enabled.

findings.category: Denial of Service / External Provider Hardening
findings.title: Live AI provider call has no explicit timeout or bulkhead in application code
findings.description: The admin AI consultation endpoint synchronously calls the provider through `chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content()` with no application-visible timeout, concurrency limit, or cancellation policy. If provider calls hang or slow down, admin threads can be tied up.
findings.evidence: The only provider guard is fallback when the API key or ChatClient is missing; no timeout-related properties or wrappers were found in `src/main/java` or `src/main/resources`.
findings.suggestedFix: Configure explicit connect/read timeouts for the Spring AI/OpenAI client and add a small concurrency limit or circuit breaker around live generation. Preserve the existing fallback/error response path.

escalations.description: Decide whether `application-docker.yml` is intended only for local smoke demos or production-like deployment. If production-like, the default database password must be removed before release.
Confirm the intended deployment topology for forwarded headers. If a reverse proxy is used, define the trusted proxy list and source-IP extraction contract.

results.summary: Performance review found no N+1 association risks, but product list/search issue avoidable duplicate count queries, DTO-only reads still materialize JPA entities, search is non-sargable for larger catalogs, and cache strategy is absent for stable product master context.

findings.title: Product listing can execute a duplicate count query
findings.description: `findAll(specification, pageable)` returns a `Page` and may already execute a count query to populate total elements. The service then calls `productRepository.count(specification)` separately, adding another count round trip on common full-page responses.
findings.evidence: List<Product> products = productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable).getContent(); followed by long totalCount = productRepository.count(specification);
findings.suggestedFix: Store the returned `Page<Product>` and use `page.getTotalElements()`: `Page<Product> page = productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable); return new ProductListResponse(page.getContent().stream().map(productMapper::toDto).toList(), page.getTotalElements());`

findings.title: Product search can execute a duplicate count query
findings.description: The search path repeats the same count-pattern risk as listing: `findAll(specification, pageable)` can compute total elements, then `count(specification)` runs the count again before response construction.
findings.evidence: List<Product> products = productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable).getContent(); followed by long totalCount = productRepository.count(specification);
findings.suggestedFix: Use a single `Page<Product>` result and read `getTotalElements()` from it. If total count is not required for a future endpoint, use `Slice`/limit-only querying to avoid count entirely.

findings.title: Product read APIs materialize managed entities for DTO-only responses
findings.description: Product list/search endpoints load `Product` entities and then map them to `ProductDto`. For DTO-only read APIs this creates entity materialization and persistence-context overhead on every request. Since current `ProductDto` includes all product columns, column reduction is limited, but projection still avoids managed entity creation.
findings.evidence: The service fetches `Product` entities via repository `findAll(...)` and maps them with `products.stream().map(productMapper::toDto).toList()`.
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce a DTO projection query or custom repository projection for product list/search, for example JPQL constructor projection into `ProductDto` or an interface projection compatible with the dynamic filters.

findings.title: Keyword search uses leading-wildcard lower LIKE predicates
findings.description: Search builds `%keyword%` predicates across manufacturer, name, category, and description. This is database-side filtering, but it is non-sargable for normal btree indexes and will trend toward full scans as product rows grow.
findings.evidence: String pattern = "%" + keyword.trim().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) + "%"; then lower(column) LIKE pattern on four fields.
findings.suggestedFix: For PostgreSQL production data, use full-text search or `pg_trgm` GIN indexes on normalized searchable text. Keep the current simple LIKE path only for small demo catalogs or H2 tests.

findings.title: AI consultation reloads stable product master context on every request
findings.description: Each AI consultation queries distinct categories and manufacturers even though product master data is seeded and changes infrequently. No Spring Cache/Redis/cache annotations were found in the backend.
findings.evidence: new AiPromptContext(productRepository.findDistinctCategories(), productRepository.findDistinctManufacturers()) is executed per consultation.
findings.suggestedFix: Cache category/manufacturer lookups with `@Cacheable` or an application-level product-master context cache, and define `@CacheEvict` when future admin product mutation is introduced.

findings.title: PostgreSQL zero-hit upsert performs an extra select after update
findings.description: The atomic upsert writes the row, then performs a repository lookup by normalized keyword to return the persisted aggregate. PostgreSQL can return the updated row directly with `RETURNING`, avoiding an extra round trip on every zero-hit record.
findings.evidence: `jdbcTemplate.update(UPSERT_SQL, ...)` is followed by `zeroHitSearchRepository.findByNormalizedKeyword(normalizedKeyword)`.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `RETURNING id, keyword, normalized_keyword, hit_count, priority, estimated_opportunity_loss, first_searched_at, last_searched_at` to the upsert SQL and map the row with `NamedParameterJdbcTemplate.queryForObject`.

findings.title: Prompt list formatting performs unnecessary list materialization and string concatenation reduction
findings.description: The prompt builder maps values, collects them into a list, streams again, then reduces with repeated string concatenation. The list is capped at 20, so impact is low, but the allocation pattern is avoidable.
findings.evidence: `.map(value -> "- " + value).toList().stream().reduce((left, right) -> left + System.lineSeparator() + right)`
findings.suggestedFix: Use `Collectors.joining(System.lineSeparator())` after the map step, with a fallback when the joined result is blank.

escalations.description: Decide whether the product catalog is expected to grow beyond demo scale. If yes, prioritize full-text/trigram search and projection work before public OSS release benchmarks.

Actuator health probes are enabled and no direct new RestTemplate() usage was found, but graceful shutdown and external dependency health coverage are incomplete.

findings.title: Live AI provider call has no retry or circuit breaker protection
findings.description: SpringAiProviderClient.generate() performs the live external AI call directly through ChatClient. There are no Resilience4j or Spring Retry annotations/configuration on this path, and pom.xml does not include a resilience dependency. A transient OpenAI/Spring AI failure therefore reaches the service on the first attempt and repeated user requests can amplify an outage instead of being governed by bounded retry and circuit breaking.
findings.evidence: Line 35 calls chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content(); rg found no @Retry, @CircuitBreaker, @RateLimiter, @TimeLimiter, @Bulkhead, resilience4j dependency, or spring-retry dependency in the target source/config.
findings.suggestedFix: Add Resilience4j Spring Boot support, configure an aiProvider instance with maxAttempts 3, exponential backoff, and circuit breaker thresholds, then wrap generate() with @Retry(name = "aiProvider", fallbackMethod = "generateFallback") and @CircuitBreaker(name = "aiProvider", fallbackMethod = "generateFallback"). The fallback should return Optional.empty() or a controlled provider-error path based on the desired API providerStatus.

findings.title: External AI call has no explicit timeout contract
findings.description: The OpenAI ChatClient/OpenAiApi bean is created without an application-owned connect/read timeout, and the live call has no Resilience4j TimeLimiter. If the provider or network stalls, the request can occupy a servlet thread until lower-level defaults intervene, which are not visible or controlled by this service configuration.
findings.evidence: OpenAiApi.builder().apiKey(...).build() and ChatClient.create(chatModel) are used without timeout properties or client customisation; application.yml only configures api-key and model for AI.
findings.suggestedFix: Expose app.ai.connect-timeout/read-timeout or Spring AI client timeout properties and wire them into the OpenAiApi underlying HTTP client where supported. Also consider @TimeLimiter(name = "aiProvider") for an overall operation deadline, with a fallback that preserves the existing degraded response behavior.

findings.title: Graceful shutdown is not enabled
findings.description: The service has server configuration but does not set server.shutdown=graceful or a shutdown phase timeout. During deployment or container termination, in-flight admin/API requests can be cut off instead of drained cleanly.
findings.evidence: The server block configures header/body/error behavior only. rg found no server.shutdown, spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, or graceful shutdown setting in main/test resource files or Dockerfile.
findings.suggestedFix: Add server.shutdown: graceful and spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s (or an SLO-appropriate value). Ensure the container orchestrator termination grace period is longer than the application shutdown timeout.

findings.title: Readiness does not cover the configured live AI dependency
findings.description: Actuator health and probe endpoints are enabled, but there is no custom HealthIndicator for the external AI provider. When AI_API_KEY is configured, the OpenAI dependency can be unavailable while /actuator/health/readiness still reports the application as ready, hiding a degraded user-facing feature from operations.
findings.evidence: management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled is true and health is exposed, but rg found no HealthIndicator implementation in src/main/java. The live dependency is SpringAiProviderClient at line 35.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an AiProviderHealthIndicator with a short bounded check or a cached/provider-status based indicator. Decide whether AI should affect readiness; if the feature is optional, expose the indicator as a separate component and keep readiness UP while surfacing degraded status through health details/metrics.

findings.title: No concurrency isolation around slow external AI calls
findings.description: The admin AI consultation endpoint can invoke a slow external provider without a semaphore or thread-pool bulkhead. Under provider slowness, concurrent admin calls can accumulate and consume request-processing capacity shared with other APIs.
findings.evidence: The provider call is executed inline in the request path and rg found no @Bulkhead or bulkhead configuration.
findings.suggestedFix: Configure a Resilience4j semaphore bulkhead for aiProvider, for example maxConcurrentCalls based on expected admin traffic, and return the existing fallback/error response when the bulkhead is full.

escalations.description: Decide whether the AI provider is operationally critical enough to fail readiness. The current product behavior has fallback/error responses, so readiness could either remain UP with a degraded component indicator or turn DOWN when live AI is required by deployment policy.
